Three Minutes to Save the Constitution
And Why the Host Hung Up

I called into The @WilkowMajority armed with nothing but the Constitution, a stopwatch, and a promise Andrew Wilkow made on air: 
“Give me three minutes—anyone—and explain how all these federal laws are constitutional.”
He set the timer.
He said, “GO.”
I began where the Framers did.

The Enclave Clause: Congress’s Municipal Sandbox
Ready? Here it is:
* I, Section 8, Clause 17 grants Congress exclusive legislative authority over the District of Columbia and all federal enclaves—military bases, post offices, federal buildings.
* Article IV, Section 3, Clause 2 doubles down: Congress governs federal territories “in all cases whatsoever.”
That’s it.
That’s the only place Congress gets to play city council.

Then came the Insular Cases (1901–1922). The Supreme Court ruled that in unincorporated territories—Puerto Rico, Guam, the Philippines—the Constitution does not follow the flag unless Congress says so.
In Downes v. Bidwell, the Court said Congress could tax Puerto Rico differently because it was not part of the constitutional compact.
(Andrew even raised this point: Why don't residents of Puerto Rico pay income tax? Guess Wilkow never read the Insular Cases) 
Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented with fire:
“The idea that this country may acquire territories anywhere upon the earth, by conquest or treaty, and hold them as mere colonies or provinces… the people inhabiting them to enjoy only such rights as Congress chooses to grant them… is wholly inconsistent with the spirit and letter, as well as with the principles, of our Constitution. … It will be an evil day for American liberty if the theory of a government outside of the supreme law of the land finds lodgment in our constitutional jurisprudence. … In short, this doctrine of legislative absolutism in the matter of acquired territory is as repugnant to the Constitution as it is to the moral sense of the American people.”
Harlan warned of a government without constitutional restraint in federal zones.
He was right.

The Federal Zone: Where 95% of Federal “Law” Actually Lives
Look at the U.S. Code.
* Title 18 (federal crimes)
* Title 21 (FDA, controlled substances)
* Title 26 (income tax)
* Title 42 (Social Security, Medicare)
No one can cite Article I, Section 8 powers over the 50 states
Why? Because they don’t apply there—unless you voluntarily step into the Federal Zone.
These are municipal laws—binding only in:
* Washington, D.C.
* Federal territories
* Federal enclaves
* Anyone who contracts in (SSN, federal employment, grants, licenses)
The Supreme Court confirmed this in Hooven & Allison Co. v. Evatt (1945), defining three meanings of “United States”:
1. The sovereign States of the Union 
2. The federal government
3. The federal zone (D.C. + territories)
Federal municipal law only has in rem jurisdiction in #3.

In the 50 states? Only if you consent.

The Taxation Trap: “But Who Pays for All This?”
Wilkow’s retort: “What gives Congress authority to tax for these extra-constitutional programs?”
Then he hung up.

Deflection is not argument.

Here’s the answer he didn’t want:

Consent. Contract. Compact.

* Social Security? States voluntarily signed on in 1935.
* Medicare? Same.
* Federal highways, education grants, Medicaid? All conditional spending—states opt in.
* Income tax? Only binds:
** Federal employees
** D.C./territory residents
** Anyone who files Form 1040 (admitting liability under territorial law)

No citizen is required to apply for a Social Security Number.
The statute itself says so: 42 U.S.C. § 405(c)(2)(B)(i)(II) — SSNs are issued only to those who request one for federal tax purposes, employment, or benefits.
You volunteer.
You apply.
You accept the benefit. You sign the contract.
That’s not tyranny.
That’s federalism.

How Do You Know Where You’re Going…
…if you don’t know where you’ve been?

The Framers never gave Congress general police power over the states.
They did give it total control over a 10-mile square and federal territories.
We’ve forgotten the difference.
We’ve let municipal law creep into sovereign states because we volunteered—one SSN, one federal grant, one 1040 at a time.

Harlan saw it coming: legislative absolutism.

And we’re living it.
Wilkow wanted a debate.
He got the truth.
And he hung up.

Maybe next time he’ll let the timer run to zero.
Because the Constitution already did.

data.raw_text:
#WxHistory |
[🧵] Typhoon Goni '20 (Rolly) became the most powerful landfalling TC on record, hitting the Philippines w/ winds up to 195mph & a pressure of 884mb. The impacts to Catanduanes was catastrophic. Extreme winds & storm surge destroyed numerous buildings & homes. Shelters were no match for Goni's winds as it blew the roofs off the buildings. 

Later on, Goni worsened the impacts to the flooding the occurred in Vietnam during the autumn. 

Goni was responsible for killing 32 & dealing over $1B in damages. Both Goni & Rolly were retired & replaced w/ Gaenari & Romina respectively. 
[1/2]
